To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) fruit species that are most attractive to primates are those that are highest in protein and lowest in fat; (2) the protein:fat ratio of fruit is more important than the total amount of either nutrient in determining fruit attractiveness to primates; and (3) fruit species that contain high amounts of protein and low amounts of fat are rare.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fruit species of BCI are not all equally attractive to the frugivores of the area and that the nutrient content of the fruits is one of the major determinants in this regard.
the macronutrients of fruits are not randomly distributed among species, and that the patterns of nutrient distribution among species are related to the feeding patterns of frugivores.
we have found that the most common fruit species in the forest are the ones most likely to be consumed by a large number of species of primates and other frugivores.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a great deal of variation in the macronutrients among fruits.
the macronutrients in fruit pulp are highly variable among species, and this variability can influence fruit choice by seed-dispersing frugivores.
there are no simple relationships among the macronutrients of the pulp of a fruit, and that there is no single fruit type that is optimal for all frugivore species.
